section_summary: This section documents the South Manchuria Railway Company's purchasing, contracting, finances, transportation network, industrial properties, and declining profitability between 1930 and 1934. Consular and diplomatic reports attribute much of the decline to depression, silver exchange, and competition from Chinese railways and ports, and connect that rivalry to the Japanese occupation of Manchuria. Later documents cover the Chinchow–Pitsuwo Railway, proposals to place the company under Japanese Army control, renewed procurement for Manchukuo and the Kwantung Army, and large railway and industrial investments.

subfiles.title: Transmittal: Purchases of the South Manchuria Railway Company
subfiles.from: William R. Langdon, American Consul, Dairen
subfiles.about: Transmits a detailed report on South Manchuria Railway Company purchases since its 1907 reorganization.
subfiles.summary: Langdon reports that annual purchases fell sharply from about ¥54.5 million to ¥19.8 million because of declining revenue and President Sengoku's economy program. He notes the collapse of American sales and the increasing predominance of Japanese and Manchurian goods, many produced by railway subsidiaries. He warns that the company's policy of favoring Japanese industry leaves poor prospects for American suppliers and asks that its confidential source material be used cautiously.

subfiles.title: Purchases of the South Manchuria Railway Company, 1907–1930
subfiles.doc_type: commercial report with statistical tables and annexes
subfiles.from: William R. Langdon, American Consul, Dairen
subfiles.about: Surveys the value, composition, sources, procedures, suppliers, and contractors involved in South Manchuria Railway Company purchasing.
subfiles.summary: The report tabulates annual purchases, merchandise classes, and countries of origin from 1907 through 1930, showing the rising share taken by Japanese and locally manufactured goods. It describes the company's nonpublic tendering system, reliance on Dairen intermediaries, direct foreign purchasing, and large building and municipal-development program. Annexes list sales by leading Dairen firms and approved building and specialist contractors throughout the railway zone and Kwantung Leased Territory. The report concludes that access through established local firms was the most effective route to company business.

subfiles.title: File note: Sengoku resignation and Uchida appointment
subfiles.about: Indexes a report on the resignation of Mitsugu Sengoku and the appointment of Count Kōsai Uchida as railway president.
subfiles.summary: The sheet cross-references another decimal-file location for a June 30 report from Japan. Its subject is the change in leadership of the South Manchuria Railway Company.

subfiles.title: Change in leadership of the South Manchuria Railway
subfiles.about: Explains Sengoku's resignation, Uchida's appointment, and the political and economic problems facing the railway.
subfiles.summary: Mitsugu Sengoku resigned on grounds of poor health and was succeeded by Count Kōsai Uchida, whose selection was intended to keep railway policy above party politics. The report identifies declining profits, competition from Chinese railways, and China's export tax on Fushun coal as major problems. It also discusses Uchida's diplomatic background and the appointment of Mitsubishi-connected Teijō Eguchi as vice president.

subfiles.title: File note: Second report on progress in Manchuria in 1930
subfiles.about: Records receipt of the railway company's second report on progress in Manchuria during 1930.
subfiles.summary: This document-file note identifies a report received October 7, 1931, and supplies a cross-reference to another decimal-file location. The substantive report itself is not reproduced on this page.

subfiles.title: File note for Geneva Telegram 239
subfiles.about: Indexes a telegram concerning Japanese accusations that China violated treaty obligations affecting railway interests in Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: The note summarizes the Japanese delegation's second communiqué to the League of Nations Council. It highlights Japanese capital in China and allegations that Chinese authorities obstructed Japanese nationals and railway interests.

subfiles.title: Telegram 239: Japanese delegation's second communiqué on Manchuria
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese claims that Chinese violations and hostility prevented troop withdrawal from Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: The Japanese delegation credits the South Manchurian Railway, Japanese troops, and extensive Japanese investment with developing Manchuria. It accuses China of treaty evasion, attacks on railway property and guards, discriminatory land policies, and mistreatment of Koreans. The communiqué asserts that Japan has no territorial designs but requires guarantees against hostile official action before withdrawing its forces.

subfiles.title: Business of the South Manchuria Railway Company
subfiles.from: William R. Langdon, American Consul, Dairen
subfiles.about: Reviews the railway company's finances and operating divisions for the year ended March 31, 1931, and assesses its prospects for 1931–32.
subfiles.summary: Net profit fell from roughly ¥46 million to ¥22 million as passenger and freight traffic, coal sales, shipping, and harbor receipts declined. The report details railway mileage and rolling stock, Dairen's harbor works, the Fushun collieries and shale-oil plant, Anshan iron production, municipal administration, and affiliated enterprises. Although the company continued capital improvements, it used reserves to maintain dividends, halted new investments, dismissed employees, and sharply curtailed purchases. Langdon argues that competition from Chinese railways and Newchwang, intensified by the silver–gold exchange disparity, posed a more serious long-term threat than the general depression.

subfiles.title: South Manchuria Railway Company general balance sheet as of March 31, 1931
subfiles.about: Presents the company's assets, liabilities, operating results, and disposition of profit for fiscal 1930–31.
subfiles.summary: The balance sheet values net assets and liabilities at approximately ¥1.116 billion and itemizes railway, harbor, mining, oil, iron, municipal, and investment properties. The profit-and-loss account shows a net profit of about ¥21.67 million, with losses in local administration and weak earnings from several industrial departments. Profit was allocated to reserves, government and public-stock dividends, officials' bonuses, and the balance carried forward.

subfiles.title: Chinese Railroad and Harbor Competition in Manchuria
subfiles.from: William R. Langdon, American Consul, Dairen
subfiles.about: Analyzes Chinese railway and port competition as a cause of the South Manchuria Railway's decline and the Sino-Japanese conflict.
subfiles.summary: Langdon contrasts falling earnings on Japanese lines with rapid gains on Chinese routes and demonstrates the Chinese system's freight-rate advantage for soybean traffic. Newchwang's exports and imports were expanding rapidly, while future linkage to the deep, ice-free port of Huludao threatened Dairen further. The despatch argues that unsuccessful negotiations over traffic division helped motivate Japan's September 18 occupation of strategic railway centers. It predicts that the conflict will not be settled until the South Manchuria Railway and Dairen are protected from Chinese competition by agreement or other means.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of the despatch on Chinese railroad and harbor competition
subfiles.to: William R. Langdon, American Consul, Dairen
subfiles.about: Acknowledges and commends Langdon's report on Chinese transportation competition in Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: The Department states that it found the information timely and valuable. It commends Langdon for his alertness to the political significance of current developments.

subfiles.title: Department memorandum on the Chinchow–Pitsuwo Railway
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.about: Summarizes a Dairen despatch and the railway company's denial of a proposed extension toward Antung.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum notes that much of the enclosed railway bulletin repeated information already known to the Department. It identifies the denial of press reports about a northeastern extension to Antung as the announcement's significant point.

subfiles.title: Chinchow–Pitsuwo Railway in the Kwantung Leased Territory
subfiles.from: John Carter Vincent, American Consul, Dairen
subfiles.about: Transmits and comments upon a South Manchuria Railway bulletin about the Chinchow–Pitsuwo line.
subfiles.summary: Vincent describes the line from Chinchow through Pitsuwo to Chengtzutung and its role in developing peanut farming, salt production, and stone quarrying. He notes a nearly completed motor road from Chengtzutung to Antung and questions the bulletin's claim that a railway over the same route would not be profitable. The despatch explains that Okura Gumi controlled the private railway, while the South Manchuria Railway held stock and probably exercised substantial influence.

subfiles.title: Bulletin on the Chinchow–Pitsuwo (Chengtzutung) Railway
subfiles.about: Describes the construction, finances, subsidies, economic effects, and proposed future of the Chinchow–Pitsuwo Railway.
subfiles.summary: The bulletin states that the 102.2-kilometre private railway was built in 1926–27 to open northeastern Kwantung to agriculture, salt production, and quarrying. An initial ¥559,000 subsidy was consumed in four years, and a later request for continued aid was first rejected, although the South Manchuria Railway subsequently reconsidered assistance. The line owned no rolling stock and rented equipment and crews from the South Manchuria Railway. The bulletin denies reports of an extension to Antung because mountainous terrain and tunneling costs would undermine commercial viability.

subfiles.title: Department memorandum on proposed military control of the South Manchuria Railway
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.about: Summarizes Embassy reporting on Japanese Army plans to reorganize and control the South Manchuria Railway.
subfiles.summary: The proposed scheme would dissolve or reorganize the railway company, amalgamate Manchurian railways, and place the resulting holding company nominally under the ambassador but effectively under Army control. The memorandum connects the plan with preparation for possible war with Russia and a broader program for nationalizing industry. It notes opposition from the Department of Overseas Affairs, industrial interests, and the press, as well as assurances that the Open Door principle would not be affected.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 584: Militarization of the South Manchuria Railway
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, United States Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports the Japanese Army's plan to place the South Manchuria Railway and related industries under military direction.
subfiles.summary: The plan contemplated transforming the company into a holding organization, returning the railway zone to Manchukuo, combining the railway with Manchukuo's system, and assigning strategic industries such as coal and iron to Army supervision. Grew explains that the Army invoked administrative unity and national defence, while observers saw preparation for war with Russia and a test of industrial militarization. General Hishikari's remarks suggested a vision of permanent Japanese control and eventual annexation of Manchukuo. Civil agencies, business leaders, and newspapers objected to the financial, treaty, industrial, and constitutional implications, leaving the Saitō cabinet in a difficult position.

subfiles.title: Purchases of the South Manchuria Railway Company
subfiles.from: Arnold Van Benschoten, American Vice Consul, Dairen
subfiles.about: Updates the 1931 purchasing report and lists the railway company's leading contractors for fiscal 1934–35.
subfiles.summary: The report states that purchases rose sharply with new railway construction and participation in industrial enterprises, while American goods—especially motor cars—accounted for about five percent of fiscal 1933–34 purchases. The company declined to furnish the detailed commodity, origin, and supplier data previously supplied confidentially. The appended contractor list contains only Japanese firms, unlike the more internationally mixed approved list of four years earlier.

subfiles.title: Balance sheet of the South Manchuria Railway Company for fiscal 1933–34
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Analyzes the company's March 31, 1934 balance sheet, capital expansion, investments, railway construction advances, and liabilities.
subfiles.summary: Total assets reached about ¥1.613 billion, though roughly ¥288 million represented uncalled stock following an increase in authorized capital from ¥440 million to ¥800 million. Fixed assets declined after transfer of the Anshan iron works to Showa Steel Works, while investments in subsidiary electric, gas, shipping, steel, chemical, petroleum, and coal companies rose substantially. The report suggests that large unadjusted advance payments concealed the construction costs of new Manchukuo railways, including the Dunhua–Tumen, Harbin–Lafa, and Keshan–Hailun lines and further projects toward Heihe and in Jehol. The surviving section also discusses increased paid-up capital, reserves, and changes in domestic and foreign bonds; the despatch continues beyond page 80.
